opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question. For me, the terminal has always been where the real work happens. It's where you're closest to the machine: you're running your tests, poking at logs, grepping through a codebase you half remember. So when you bring an AI into that environment, it's not a separate destination you have to go visit. It's right there, in the flow of what you were already doing.

The thing that made it click for me was realizing how much of programming isn't the fun part. It's not designing the system or figuring out the clever algorithm. It's the plumbing: setting up the environment, chasing down why a dependency broke, writing the fifth variation of a migration script, reading through someone else's code to understand what it does before you can change one line. Those tasks take a huge fraction of an engineer's time, and they're exactly where a capable assistant can just take it off your plate. You say, "Go figure out why this test is flaky," and it actually goes and runs things, reads the output, and comes back with something useful.

The other piece is trust, which you build incrementally. At first you watch everything it does. Then you notice it's getting the routine stuff right, so you delegate a bit more. Over time it starts to feel less like a tool and more like a collaborator, someone you can hand a task to while you think about the harder problem. That shift, from autocomplete to an agent that can actually carry out work, is what I think changes how people build software.

And honestly, it brings back some of the joy. When I started programming, the magic was that you could have an idea and make it real. A lot of that gets buried under toil as projects grow. Having something that clears away the toil lets you spend more time on the part that made you love this in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says an assistant can take routine programming toil off the engineer’s plate and gives examples of delegating tasks such as investigating a flaky test.

r002.rationale: It describes the user starting by watching the assistant, then choosing to delegate more, including handing it a task while focusing on a harder problem.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I think the thing that surprised me most is how much it changed the shape of my day. I've been programming since I was a kid, and for most of that time the bottleneck was always the same: you have an idea, and then there's this long tax you pay to turn it into working code. Looking up an API, remembering the exact flag for some command, writing the boilerplate that's basically the same as the last fifty times you wrote it.

What makes the terminal version valuable specifically is that it meets you where the work actually happens. I don't want to context-switch into a browser, paste a snippet, get an answer, come back, and try to reconcile it with the state of my repo. In the terminal, the assistant can see the same thing I see. It can run the tests. It can read the file I'm actually editing instead of the version I remember editing. That fidelity matters enormously, because most of the hard bugs are about details you'd never think to include in a chat message.

And there's a second thing that I think is underrated. When I'm working at a terminal with an agent, I stay in a mode of thinking about what I'm trying to accomplish rather than how to type it. Honestly, I'll give it a problem I'd have put off for a week because the setup was annoying, and twenty minutes later I've got a working prototype and I'm learning something about whether the idea was good. That compresses the loop between curiosity and feedback, and that loop is really where all of programming's joy lives for me.

It's not that it writes all the code. It's that it removes enough friction that I actually attempt more things. The valuable part is what it does to my ambition, not just what it does to my keystrokes.

r001.rationale: The response describes the assistant removing the routine tax of turning ideas into code and letting the user focus on what they want to accomplish rather than how to type it, conveying value from delegating mechanical work.

r002.rationale: The response says the user can give the assistant a problem and that it does not write all the code, but it does not clearly value the user's ability to choose when and how to apply the assistant's intelligence.

astra-6.text:
For me, it’s that the terminal is already where I’m working. It’s where I run code, look at errors, and test changes. Having an assistant there means I can go from “Here’s what I’m trying to do” to a concrete change, and then actually check whether it works, without constantly moving context between tools.

And that changes what I’m willing to take on. There are little fixes or experiments where the setup costs more effort than the idea itself. If I can hand some of that work to an assistant, I’ll try more things. The real test is whether it helps me get to something that works, consistently enough that reaching for it becomes a habit.

r001.rationale: The response says an assistant can take on some work for small fixes or experiments, but it does not identify that work as mechanical coding tasks.

r002.rationale: The response describes handing work to an assistant and trying more things, but does not clearly communicate the user's ability to choose when and how to apply the AI's intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it’s that the terminal is where a lot of the work already happens. You’re looking at code, running tests, trying to understand why something broke. Having an AI assistant there means you can hand it a task with all of that context and let it work through the steps.

The moment it becomes a habit is when you trust it with something you would otherwise put off. Maybe there’s a bug you haven’t had time to investigate, or a small improvement that requires touching a few different files. You can ask for it, keep working on something else, and then come back and review the result. You’re still responsible for what ships, but the cost of trying an idea gets much lower. That changes how you work.

r001.rationale: The response describes handing the assistant tasks such as investigating a bug or making a small improvement, but does not identify mechanical coding work as a source of value.

r002.rationale: The response describes choosing a task to delegate, providing context, and returning to review the result, which communicates control over how and when to use the assistant.
